item.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
item.author: Guardian sport
item.content:encoded: Florian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion on Tyneside and Chelsea face litmus test at ArsenalFlorian Wirtz is easing himself into his second season at Liverpool after a forgettable first. There were signs of promise against Nottingham Forest, where he set up the second equaliser and would have had a goal of his own if not for an offside in the buildup. It is clear the German needs to become more influential as a No 10 given the quality of players he has around him, especially after the expensive arrival of Bradley Barcola this week. Bruno Fernandes showed there is plenty of fun for an attacking midfielder to have against Ipswich and Wirtz can follow suit as a protagonist. Liverpool have drawn both their opening fixtures 2-2 and need something to kickstart their campaign, with a Friday night visit to promoted opposition a fine place to start. Wirtz should cause problems but, if he does not, the internal competition will be after his spot. Ipswich v Liverpool (Friday 8pm, all times BST)Newcastle v Bournemouth (Saturday 12.30pm)Brentford v Sunderland (Saturday 3pm)Continue reading...

item.title: Tactically perfect and on the offensive like never before – Enric Mas drops all his rivals at the Vuelta a España, but he must keep attacking – Analysis
item.content:encoded: In years gone by, the words Movistar and tactical masterclass were incompatible, polar opposites, an oxymoron even. Rightly questioned on several occasions for how they approached the biggest races and utilised their multiple leaders, on today's stage 12 of the Vuelta a España, the Spanish team completely flipped the script, executing a perfect plan with their figurehead Enric Mas gaining time on all of his rivals and strengthening his hold on the GC leader's red jersey.And for Mas too, this 2026 race has been a complete reversal of his previous outcomes and experiences from the Vuelta. Always the bridesmaid, Mas is a three-time runner-up and has finished in the top six on six occasions at the Vuelta, but before this ongoing edition, he had never really looked like he would win his home race.Even in the years when he was second best, the closest Mas ever got to the top step of the podium was in 2018, finishing 1:46 behind Simon Yates. Primož Roglič was almost five minutes ahead of him in 2021, and Remco Evenepoel too was two minutes ahead by the time they reached Madrid in 2022.Fittingly, Mas' lead is now one second off his narrowest losing margin, and that is to Roglič, the rider who for years has had his number at the Vuelta. With nine stages to go, he is in the driving seat, and 2026 becoming the year of Enric Mas is looking more and more like a reality every time the race summits a tough climb; such is his superiority going uphill as it stands.Powered partially by the maillot rojo on his shoulders, Mas looked every bit the assured race leader he's long threatened to become, but never quite managed, on stage 12. When the moment came on the final climb to Calar Alto to get his tactics just right, he and Movistar made no mistake, but the seeds were sown much earlier in the day.Four climbs of increasing difficulty lining the 166km route before the finale allowed ample time for a breakaway to form on Thursday, with 30 riders eventually getting up the road after around 40km of attacking.With the irregularity of the gradients on the finale climb to Calar Alto, having satellite riders up the road was the best tactic for all of those hoping to make their mark in the GC, and the makeup of the 30 riders highlighted that.Luke Tuckwell represented Roglič's Red Bull team. Decathlon CMA CGM had Léo Bisiaux up the road to potentially help third-place Felix Gall later on, while Netcompany Ineos had two riders in Jack Haig and Axel Laurance as possible options for Oscar Onley to bridge across to and improve his fourth position. Race leader Mas' Movistar team hadn't missed out either, putting Pablo Castrillo and Raúl García Pierna in the move.From here, Movistar settled into controlling the gap, which ballooned out to more than seven minutes with two of their riders unable to help, but even as the stage win went up the road, they never lost control.Onto the second-to-last climb, they were hit with a surprise attack from former teammate Richard Carapaz towards the top of the Alto de Velefique, and with only one teammate left for Mas in the peloton.Ivan Romeo toiled away at the front to bring him back before the summit, and by the time the descent and the final climb arrived, Castrillo was on his way back to provide sustenance and support for Mas and his only remaining domestique.Decathlon soon took over to pace for Gall, but this is where Mas came into his own, never looking uncomfortable under the pressure applied by the French team, who have consistently looked stronger as a climbing outfit throughout this Vuelta.Once Gall made his move, as was the case at Alto de Aitana on stage 9, Mas was more than up to the task, sitting in his wheel with Roglič the only other rider able to follow. Once again, he was in control, but there was still work to do.Speaking to on Wednesday, Roglič's lead sports director at this Vuelta, Sven Vanthourenhout, had said that Mas making a move was exactly what he was expecting. And with the stage 18 time trial a week from today making the 1:18 lead he started stage 12 with seem much smaller in reality, venturing out of his comfort zone is necessary for Mas.Having been labelled boring or perhaps been guilty of not believing he can win the biggest races in the past for his lack of attacking bravery, on this occasion, while defence of red is his main aim, the best form of that must be attack."Mas knows that even if it is still a nice 1:00 to 1:30 advantage on his contenders, it's still not enough to win the Vuelta," said Vanthourenhout. "So for sure he's also going to try it now in that second week to take some seconds or do some moves."Attack he did, and with that second satellite rider García Pierna still up the road to give Mas a final assist, by the time they reached the finish line, Mas had gained 27 seconds, now with a 1:45 lead over Roglič and a 2:06 gap to Gall.While the flat 32km race against the clock on stage 18 remains very much in favour of Roglič, those extra almost 30 seconds could prove vital before the duo of final climbing stages.Realistically, a top-form Roglič could still bring that back, but having been hit by a driver and crashed before the race, coming good in the third is by no means certain for the four-time winner, and if anything, the opposite – a collapse – is more likely.For Gall, who is similarly a poor time trialist, Mas won't have much to worry about if he can maintain his climbing superiority, but it is his long-term rival who remains the biggest threat. But he has another chance to extend his lead in two days to Sierra de la Frontera, and the Mas and Movistar we saw today look almost guaranteed to try and capitalise on their current authority.Mas may have inherited red after the misfortune of Pogačar, but he's only done everything in his power to make it his since, and it looks like he might just win it after all. Rewind 12 months from now, and Mas at 30 seemed like he had run out of chances to put on a performance like he's currently in the midst of – having just abandoned the Tour, severe varicose vein formations and thrombophlebitis in his left leg left him requiring surgery.He missed last year's Vuelta, the first since 2019 he hadn't been a part of, but he's returned as an Enric Mas we haven't seen before. Perhaps he too is starting to believe, even if there's a long way and three brutal summit finishes still to contend with, but for the moment, Mas looks more like he'll conquer them than see his incredible run come to an end.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Meet Yostin Peña, the man of the hour in the Yankees’ system
item.author: Andrés Chávez
item.content:encoded: The Yankees have plenty of talent in their minor league affiliates, so much so that young outfielder Yostin Peña, arguably the hottest hitter in the entire organization, isn’t yet ranked in MLB Pipeline’s top 30 prospects.Peña, signed last December after issues regarding his age documentation surfaced and scuttled his deal with the St. Louis Cardinals, made quick work of the Dominican Summer League, slashing a robust .375/.457/.646 with eight homers, 27 stolen bases, and a 150 wRC+ in 37 games, before earning a promotion to Single-A.There, the 18-year-old phenom has posted a brilliant .355/.419/.605 line with five round-trippers, seven thefts, and a 161 wRC+ in 18 games through Tuesday. Between the two levels, the dynamic talent has 13 dingers, 34 steals, and a 154 wRC+.Peña has some of the most exciting raw tools you will see in the low minors, and an incredible frame for such a young prospect: he is 6’4” and is listed at 205 lb. Evidently, speed and athleticism are both plus, as is his raw power.What has the industry said about him recently? In a fantasy baseball roundup, the folks at Baseball America said that Peña is ‘the highest-ranked hitting prospect still in Low-A. With excellent power for his age, a better-than-average in-zone contact rate and 15-to-20 stolen base potential, Peña is a fascinating blend of power, speed and fantasy upside.’That’s nice for our fantasy baseball community, but what about as a real-life report? Sam Dyksra and Jonathan Mayo of MLB Pipeline recently reviewed the hottest hitter in each team’s farm system, and of course Peña’s name came up when they discussed the Yankees. Here’s what they wrote on August 26:At 18 years old, Pena was a bit on the older side for the Dominican Summer League, where he opened the season, but on July 28, he skipped the FCL to get a promotion to Single-A Tampa and hasn’t looked back since. The 6-foot-4 right-handed slugger has hit .358/.389/.597 with four homers in his first 15 games with the Tarpons. (Three of those four dingers have come in the last week alone.) His big-time power (113.6 mph max exit velocity, 108.2 90th-percentile EV in the FSL) is his most intriguing asset, though a high chase rate brings some cause for concern as he sees more full-season pitching.As you can see, those are some impressive exit velocities. Considering that he can still fill out his frame with muscle and thump, his raw power potential is very scary. It’s important to remember that he is still very young and raw, and given his contact issues and propensity to chase pitches out of the zone, he probably won’t be a fast riser who will get to Triple-A in the first half of 2027.Speaking of his high chase rate, Peña’s 39.7 O-Swing% is quite high. Additionally, he has a 16.1 SwStr%, also elevated. Both marks would rank near the bottom of the league in the majors, and this is against Single-A pitching. Stats don’t actually mean much since it’s just 18 games, but it’s something to keep an eye on. Amazingly, his 17.4 percent strikeout rate in those 18 Single-A games is not that bad, but that look under the hood suggests it could be much worse.Despite his less-than-ideal approach and contact profile, Peña is an exciting prospect, indeed. Those who have seen him play believe he has superstar potential, but he needs to conquer some demons first. It’s nothing uncommon when talking about a prospect his age, though. The range of outcomes is broad here, but if Peña hits his lofty ceiling, watch out.

item.title: 'We'll keep on fighting' - Vuelta a España an uphill battle for Primož Roglič after Enric Mas gains time on Calar Alto
item.content:encoded: Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe have not given up on the idea of winning the Vuelta a España by a long shot, but they recognised that for their leader Primož Roglič, who was once again dropped by Enric Mas (Movistar) on a second straight summit finish, things are looking increasingly complicated.Almost as soon as Mas attacked at around 12 kilometres to go during the stage 12 summit finish at Calar Alto, Roglič settled into his own pace, and rather than then regaining ground as he did solo on the Spaniard on stage 9 to Aitana, this time he seemed more in need of allies to limit the damage.Hard work by Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM), as much to distance other GC rivals like Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) to try to regain ground on Mas, proved hugely beneficial. Close to the summit, the presence of teammate Luke Tuckwell, as well as the regrouping with some of Gall's teammates, all helped keep Roglič from leaking too much time.By the summit, Mas' advantage of 40 seconds at one point had shrunk to just 27, which will give Roglič some encouragement for the days to come. However, his loss on the summit of Calar Alto was still more than double his 12 second loss at Aitana.Whatever Roglič achieves between here and Granada a week on Sunday, it must be remembered that he started the Vuelta still suffering from his major training accident. Merely being able to fight for the Vuelta GC is a massive achievement. Given that so much has now become possible for Roglič, including a record-breaking fifth Vuelta a España win, there could well be some frustration that he is not quite hitting the high notes he needs.The Slovenian star's grasp on the podium looks now like a virtual certainty, and with the gap now up to 1:45 on Mas, the top spot overall, if not out of reach, is growing increasingly distant."From now on, every time we lose, we're not happy with that. Mas just showed that he's again one of the strongest riders here in the bunch, so we also need to accept this," Red Bull sports director Sven Vanthourenhout said at the summit in brief declarations to the media.Roglič is widely expected to pull back a lot of time on Mas in the flat 32km time trial on stage 18, but Vanhourenhout's concern that an already uphill task was growing increasingly steep in nature."I'm not going say a clear number on that," Vanthourenhout said when asked how much time he thought Roglič could lose before it became impossible to beat Mas. "But let's say that from now on, every time we lose, it's not the best."Roglič's next opportunity to outduel Mas will likely come on the Alto de la Pandera in Jaén on Saturday, the same climb where he began his comeback against eventual winner Remco Evenepoel in the 2022 Vuelta, only to then crash out a few days later. Then, as now, the ascent dubbed 'The Angliru of the South' will likely be another pivotal moment in his battle for another overall victory.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Back from injury, RailRiders reliever MacGregor making up for lost time
item.author: Scott Walsh
item.content:encoded: Travis MacGregor came within one pitch of an immaculate inning in the top of the first Aug. 23 at PNC Field in northeastern Pennsylvania against the Charlotte Knights, Triple-A affiliate of the Chicago White Sox.Forced to make a spot start for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, the 28-year-old right-hander struck out Rikuu Nishida on three pitches leading off the game. Then, he fanned Junior Perez on three pitches. He threw two strikes to Edgar Quero before Quero spoiled the bid by flying out to center field.It was part of a perfect three-inning performance with four strikeouts and helped send the RailRiders on their way to a 9-5 victory. MacGregor is pitching after starting the season on the 60-day injured list due to a shoulder injury suffered early in spring training. Since being activated Aug. 13, he has appeared in five games for the RailRiders. He allowed a run in his first game Aug. 13 at Lehigh Valley, but has not given up a run in the other four outings. He has 13 strikeouts in 9.2 innings. Signed by the Yankees to a minor-league contract in December as a free agent, the injury prevented MacGregor from showing his new team what he can do. He is trying to make up for lost time. “Any time you come to a new organization, you want to be able to showcase what you’re able to do,” MacGregor said. “Having to sit out for this long a time certainly was a little frustrating. But I’ve got a month left in the season pretty much to try to showcase my abilities. We’ll see what happens for the rest of the year.”At the same time, he has to be careful not to do too much lest he reinjure himself.“When I say showcase my abilities, I mean going out there and playing the way I play,” he said. “They liked something. They brought me in for a reason. I just have to go out there and play my game and showcase me for the amount of time I have. You can’t put too much pressure on yourself to try to make anything happen. That’s out of your control. I just have to make sure I’m prepared for each game that comes.”This is MacGregor’s ninth minor-league season and he has a career record of 20-37 with eight saves and a 4.62 ERA in 238 games with 552 strikeouts in 541.2 innings. He was selected out of high school by the Pittsburgh Pirates in the second round (68th overall) of the 2016 MLB Draft. He was with the Pirates organization from 2016-18 and 2021-23, missing all of the 2019 season due to Tommy John surgery and the 2020 campaign due to the COVID-19 pandemic.He signed with the Los Angeles Angels as a free agent for 2024 and spent one season in their system. In 2025, he signed as a free agent with the Texas Rangers and pitched at Double-A before being released at the end of July. He was picked up by the Milwaukee Brewers in August and finished the season in Double-A. He again became a free agent and was signed by the Yankees. “It’s been a fantastic experience,” MacGregor said. “I’ve really enjoyed getting to know all the players and staff members, the coaches. Everyone’s been great. It’s the New York Yankees. They’re talked of highly and certainly met the standards they set for themselves. I’ve really enjoyed my time here so far.”Unfortunately, his time with the Yankees got off to a rough start due to the injury in spring training. Beginning at the end of July, he made three rehab appearances with the Single-A Tampa Tarpons and one with the High-A Hudson Valley Renegades before joining the RailRiders.“Anytime anybody comes off an injury, you’re wanting to try it out or feel it out for the first couple of pitches or outings,” MacGregor said. “But you’ve done so much preparation beforehand that you have to have confidence that you’re good to go. I’ve been throwing bullpens, throwing lives, stuff like that beforehand. I knew I was in good shape.”This is not MacGregor’s first time in Triple-A. He made it to the highest level of the minors with the Pirates organization, as well as with the Angels. He has yet to make that next step to the major leagues, however.“I wouldn’t say anything preventing me. Maybe just some unfortunate timing on things,” MacGregor said. “I’m just grateful to be playing any chance that I get. I’m confident my day will come. Until then, I’ll just be where my feet are and take care of business every day.”Alexander Cornielle became the latest member of the RailRiders to earn an International League weekly award when the righthander was named Pitcher of the Week for the period of Aug. 24-30. He was honored for his shutout performance Aug. 28 at Worcester, going eight innings — a season-high for a RailRiders pitcher — and allowing just two hits with two walks and six strikeouts in a 2-0 win. It was the team’s ninth shutout of the season.Since coming off the 60-day injured list and joining the RailRiders in June, Cornielle is 5-3 in 14 games (13 starts) with a 2.70 earned-run average and 59 strikeouts in 60 innings. However, in August, he was 2-1 in five starts with a 1.50 ERA and 25 strikeouts in 24 innings.Cornielle joins Brendan Beck as RailRiders to be named IL Pitcher of the Week this season; Beck won the award three times (May 11-17, June 1-8, July 20-26) and also was chosen IL Pitcher of the Month for June. Yanquiel Fernandez (May 18-24) and Tyler Hardman (July 6-12) were selected IL Player of the Week this season.

item.title: 'It was an attack in my style' - Richard Carapaz gambles on long-distance move on Vuelta a España high mountain stage
item.content:encoded: It didn't work, but it certainly looked good while it lasted. When Richard Carapaz blasted off from the GC group on the second-to-last climb of Velefique on stage 12 of the Vuelta a España, it sparked instant speculation amongst race watchers.Was this the kind of long-distance move that could see Carapaz make an unexpected but entirely feasible challenge for the overall - similar to the one that had netted him the Giro d'Italia in 2019 whilst the main pre-race contenders simply marked each other? Was it going to force former teammate and race leader Enric Mas to chase him down?Running more than three minutes down before the mammoth mountain stage, it was not at all certain what Carapaz's attack could actually achieve, but for a few kilometres, as he quickly gained 30 seconds on the GC group, down at that point to just one support rider for Mas, it looked as if the 2026 Vuelta could have taken yet another unexpected turn.Finally, it didn't happen, as the 2026 Tour de France King of the Mountains and Alpe d'Huez stage winner lost momentum and was reeled in. But Carapaz still had enough energy to make ninth on the stage in the same group as Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) and Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) and move up to fourth overall. All in all, not such a bad day's work."I knew it was a hard day, but I wanted to attack from a way out to see who responded," Carapaz told reporters at the Calar Alto summit between swigs of recovery drinks and donning a race jacket for the long descent back to the team bus."It was a good move, I wanted to get as much time as possible, because I knew it was a very steady climb with the easy part later on towards the top.""It didn't work out, but I'm very pleased all the same, and we'll see what happens. Day by day. It was an attack in my style."Carapaz said that after being reeled back in, when the attacks by Felix Gall and then Enric Mas materialised on the Calar Alto, rather than try to follow, his best option was to save energy and not risk going too deep. His tactic paid off there, too, as he moved up to fourth overall, albeit at a now more distant 3:53 on Mas."It was all about continuing at my pace for as long as possible, and that was it - I got there," he said. "I know it's tough to recover each day on a Grand Tour, but I will keep trying in what's left of this race."If Carapaz seems to be racing as if he has nothing to lose, it could be argued that's because he hasn't. After winning two stages of the Tour and the King of the Mountains jersey following a very difficult start to the year, the racer from Ecuador has more than fulfilled his targets for 2026. But as a rider who can't resist a chance to test the waters and see what will happen, he's definitely going to try to continue to be a factor in the Vuelta as well, albeit purely for the hell of it.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'We said that we are playing PlayStation' – Breaking Pogačar's record, Jakob Omrzel becomes Slovenia's youngest Grand Tour stage winner at Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: Slovenian riders winning on mountain-top finishes at the Vuelta a España is nothing out of the ordinary; Primož Roglič has been doing that for years, and before he crashed out, Tadej Pogačar had done similarly in his limited appearances. But stage 12 of the Vuelta saw a new name from the Central European nation, which has come to dominate the current cycling era, come to the fore: Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious).With a dominant solo performance from the breakaway, the youngest rider at the 2026 race earned himself a maiden stage win on debut, but also beat Pogačar's benchmark to become Slovenia's youngest-ever Grand Tour stage winner, and became the second-youngest stage winner in Vuelta history after Celestino Prieto in 1981."I mean, it's an incredible statistic; it doesn't mean anything specific," said a nonchalant Omrzel as he sat down for his post-race press conference. "I still need to work hard, and it's a nice statistic to achieve, but that's also it."Also asked about it in his flash winners interview, he reiterated his point: "That's just a statistic; it doesn't mean anything else, but it's a nice statistic."Clearly not overly interested in the comparisons to his compatriots and instead wanting to be his own rider, not the next Pogačar or Roglič, Omrzel naturally still had to field questions about the two greats who have come before him."The best guys in Slovenia in history, and I mean, Pogi is Pogi; there's not much more to say. Primož also, how much he achieved in his career is just something unbelievable," he said. "For sure, they are both role models."Even if he doesn't want to be compared to Pogačar, the way in which he rode the finale is going to make the comparisons seem fair, taking on the final 12km alone and appearing not to be struggling after he distanced Urko Berrade – which he then confirmed at the finish with a warranted level of confidence."I'm not surprised because I know how much work I put in, and I knew that these days were going to come sooner or later. But for sure, I was not expecting 100% to do it on my first Grand Tour," said Omrzel."So, I mean, I still can't believe what I did, but I felt super good. I'm still feeling OK. I'm not tired, so I don't know, I'm just enjoying it at the moment."He went on to further detail the ease with which Bahrain Victorious dominated the 30-man breakaway on stage 12 by comparing it to playing a video game. With Pello Bilbao putting in a solid shift on his final Grand Tour appearance, Santiago Buitrago strengthening his hold on the KOM jersey, Omrzel not only had experienced support alongside him before going off on his own, but his team were able to tick off several goals in one stage."Actually, the team behind us is really great. As riders, we understand each other really well, and at the moment, we are working so well together. The whole team is just perfection," said Omrzel."We said that we are playing PlayStation, and that's what we are doing at the moment! What we want, we do. We go in the breakaway with Pello [Bilbao], Santi Buitrago], and the other guys. It's just amazing, and I'm really proud of that."As a Baby Giro winner and top prospect coming out of the under-23 ranks, Omrzel seemed destined for success as a pro, but perhaps not this quickly. Even as their current superstars are nearing the latter years of their careers, Roglič is now 36, and Pogačar is turning 28 later this month; Slovenia likely have their next figurehead in Omrzel.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: F1 teams agree plan to cut race distances for 2027
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 races are set to be shorter in 2027, with teams having agreed a plan to cut race distances across the board from 305km to 290km.In the wake of changes being made to the regulations to stop cars being so energy-starved, fuel flow rates are being increased for next year.But the move to improve the spectacle has triggered other headaches for teams, because more fuel going through the engine means more is needed to complete a race distance.That was a problem for teams that had built their current fuel tank sizes around the 2026 requirements and did not want to make an all-new car for next season.Allowance has been made in the cost cap to give teams that were planning to carry over their chassis some extra spending freedom to make modifications, but alongside this were also moves to minimise the distance cars were expected to run.Once the fuel-flow tweak had been agreed, discussions opened about potentially reducing some race distances by a couple of laps, with a further change being made in limiting drivers to just a single formation lap before the grid.But amid the talks with teams about which races needed to be targeted for adjustment, it became clear that there could be some unintended consequences if there was a variety of race distances throughout the season.It is understood that there was a risk of some events turning into fuel-economy runs.So, following dialogue between the FIA and teams, it was agreed that it would be better to have a universal distance for a grand prix throughout the season, as there is now.As first reported by Autoracer.it, this idea has now received unanimous support from teams so moves are in play to have it added to the rulebook.For years now, F1 race distances have been the fewest number of laps required to exceed 305km. The only exception to this (beyond when grands prix start behind the safety car) is the Monaco GP, which runs to 260km.The change agreed by teams for next year would result in all races (apart from Monaco) being reduced to around 290km - so will pull the events back by around three laps.While the change in distance has been supported by teams, it still needs to go through a formal process before it is put into the 2027 sporting regulations.This means revised regulations need to be proposed to the F1 Commission, which is made up of teams, the FIA and FOM. Once approved there, it will then need ratification by the FIA's World Motor Sport Council.It is understood that the reduction in race distance is currently only agreed for next season because of the compromise caused by the change of power unit rules at such a late stage.However, teams may decide to keep it at that level for longer if it is found that the additional fuel-flow changes planned for 2028 cause further trouble.

item.title: 'He doesn't always have these kinds of legs' - Enric Mas boosts overall lead in Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: Enric Mas took an important, if not decisive, step towards overall victory in the Vuelta a España on stage 12 to Calar Alto. After blasting off 11 kilometres from the finish and then fending off a group of chasers including key rivals Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe).Sixth on the first of four summit finishes in the last two weeks, Mas' move gave the Spaniard a 26-second advantage over Gall and Roglič, with his overall margin now stretching to 1:45 over the Slovenian.That advantage is beginning to look significant, if not yet definitive. In fact, that gap could have been greater had Roglič, the 2026 Giro d'Italia podium finisher and four-time Vuelta a España champion, not combined to join forces to limit the damage and also been able to count on some strong support near the summit from teammates from the early break.But Mas' transformation into a far more aggressive racer than in the past, combined with some notable teamwork by Movistar, helped tip the balance in his favour nonetheless for a second straight summit finish. The result wasn't a knock-out blow, but it reconfirmed his current superiority as the Vuelta's best climber. Equally crucially, it has provided another big morale boost to a rider whose upper limit has often been seen as the podium of a Grand Tour, but never the highest place of all."What has happened to the Enric of old?" one experienced cycling journalist asked Mas in his race leader's press conference, referring to the change in mentality or raising of the bar the Movistar rider has managed to achieve."Today he's been trying to win the Vuelta," Mas responded, playing along with the idea of talking about himself in the third person. "I hope you enjoy this version of Enric, he doesn't always have these kinds of legs, so let's enjoy it."Mas has always been one to play down his ambitions, even if he recognised to Eurosport post-stage that he was beginning to feel he was maybe in the form of his life - "it's possible" - he said. His attack at 10 kilometres from the summit had all the feel of someone willing to throw caution to the wind, in what constitutes a radical change of approach for the usually much more conservative racer.However, Mas insisted that despite the spontaneous feel of his move, coming when Gall had burned through his domestiques once again and then run out of energy himself and when Roglič was simply following wheels, it had all gone according to the pre-planned script."We did what was possible to get the maximum possible; we have to be pleased with what we've got," Mas said. "The plan we had worked out before the stage worked perfectly and everything we wanted to happen, happened."I had thought about attacking a little bit earlier, maybe a bit before, where it was harder. But what we did and where we went for it, worked out fine."Mas' teammates put in a huge effort to ensure the Spanish star could benefit as much as possible from their work, with Ivan Romeo doing a near single-handed job managing the favourites on the upper slopes of the Velefique, with Pablo Castrillo dropping back from the break for some extra support just when Romeo was flagging. Then after Gall and Decathlon had shredded the GC field on Calar Alto's tougher first half in a very similar way to how they pulled back the break on the Aitana four days ago, Mas' attack enabled him to bridge across to teammate Raúl García Pierna.Despite not being an out-and-out climber, the former national time trial champion was able to keep Mas forward momentum going, with the Spaniard pushing out the gap on the chase group of Roglič and Gall to nearly 40 seconds. Once García Pierna cracked, it was up to Mas again to keep driving on alone in the closing kilometres, tipping the balance in his favour for good once again, just as he had done on Aitana."It's a pity that we don't have Cian [Uijtdebroeks] here as well, but the circumstances are what they are," Mas said, indirectly referring to the Belgian teammate's first week abandon after an early crash."The rest of the team divided up the hard work perfectly, though, and we got the result we wanted. The most important thing is how we worked together, and at the same time I'm feeling more and more motivated and positive."Mas was equally upbeat about the upcoming challenges, with another major mountain top finish on La Pandera on stage 14 preceding the crunch time trial in Jerez de la Frontera four days before the finish. It has been estimated that Roglič could pull back as much as two minutes there in the 34-kilometre TT. Quite apart from the continuing uncertainty regarding Roglič's underlying condition, if Mas continues to open up the gaps in the mountains as he has done up to now, the Spaniard may still have the upper hand come what may."I'm feeling confident whatever happens," Mas said. "Of course we have to be aware that Primož is a former Olympic Time Trial Champion [in 2021] but we have to focus on whatever we can do.""I have a good advantage now, but there's a long way to go yet and three more summit finishes to go as well. Above all, we have to enjoy this."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Everything we learned on day one at F1's Italian GP
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: No circuit is more synonymous with Formula 1 engine performance than Italian Grand Prix host Monza.So is it any wonder talk of slipstreams (and associated tactics), engine upgrades, and even the raceability of these 2026 F1 cars dominated conversations in the paddock on Thursday?Here are the biggest takeaways ahead of the on-track action kicking off on Friday:Antonelli's willing to tow RussellKimi Antonelli will start from the back of the Monza grid whatever happens in qualifying thanks to a power unit penalty. That means he's got nothing tangible to fight for in terms of starting position in qualifying, and on a weekend where slipstreaming is expected to be beneficial he's willing to help out team-mate, and title rival, George Russell if asked. (Something that the non-engine-penalised Charles Leclerc will also do for Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton.)"It has been discussed with the team, and yes we have agreed on a few things," said Antonelli, when asked by The Race if he's willing to tow Russell. "So let's see how the session develops."If the team will ask me to do so, I will do it. Because obviously I'm not fighting for...Of course, I will still be happy to do pole, but I'm starting at the back so if I could do anything to to help the team, I will do."Starting from the back gives Antonelli an unusual challenge in a season where he's usually started at or near the front, but he argued that "in some ways it helps to release pressure" and that he's "very free mentally".Of course, that's easy to say, and limiting the damage will be a test of his mental strength. Monza will be truer test of Honda's latest engineFernando Alonso remains coy on his own F1 future, but he thinks Monza will provide a much clearer picture as regards the step Honda's taken with its latest F1 engine upgrade.Alonso called his ninth-place finish at Zandvoort a "nice boost" for Aston Martin, helping validate the development direction taken with the B-spec chassis and suggesting "eventually we will be one of the fastest in the corners", but he said the new engine fitted for Zandvoort "was not a big improvement, to be honest"."The driveability was a problem and the extra power was difficult to feel in Zandvoort," Alonso added."Maybe Monza is going to be a more true test for the engine, but still a long way to go - and we need to improve in both ends, in chassis and on engine for next year, it's a must."Alonso felt the return to the standard weekend format of three practice sessions at Monza will further aid that process and he said he has "100% trust" Honda will eventually crack the code."We just need to shortcut somehow that process," he added."Unfortunately, we started with the wrong foot and we started with this set of regulations not at the level that we wanted, but I have no doubts that they will get there."As I said many times we don't want to wait five years like they did last time, or six years. We want to do it in two years or three years maximum." Audi plays gear-ratio joker that McLaren's declinedAudi has taken its one permitted opportunity to change its gear ratios during the 2026 season, a move McLaren revealed it declined to make earlier this year.Teams only get one joker, but there's a cost involved in reconfiguring them that put McLaren off doing so - despite knowing it had erroneously picked gear ratios that were too short compared to engine supplier Mercedes before the season began.Audi has taken its joker, though, as it looks to improve a weakness with its first F1 engine."This change we have made, it was something we spotted quite early in the year, and I think it's just, again, for overall driveability, that's the main thing we have been working with our engine through the whole year now," Gabriel Bortoleto explained."I don't think it's going to improve our starts massively, if I'm very honest, but I think it's going to help us overall to be a bit more consistent on the performance of the starts, maybe."Also in wet conditions, in dry conditions, the way the gears are going to work is probably going to help us a little bit on keeping the car a little bit more stable."For Audi, it wasn't a case of having too short or too long a gear ratio, but was more about adjusting the steps between them to try and improve driveability. While Ferrari is introducing its upgraded 'ADUO 2' specification engine at Monza, courtesy of the ruling of F1's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities ranking, Ollie Bearman's Haas is the only customer car that will run it.That's because Ferrari could only supply enough of its upgraded power units for Haas and Cadillac to have one each, putting both teams in an uncomfortable position.Cadillac elected not to run it, but Haas, also debuting a sizeable aerodynamic upgrade at Monza, will do so with Bearman."Yeah, of course that's part of the consideration," team principal Ayao Komatsu said when asked if championship position (Bearman has 18 points to Ocon's three) played a role."But, again, the last two, let's say, not aerodynamic upgrades, but items we had, like CI [Carbon Industrie] brakes test, Esteban was actually struggling more on the brake locking etc so considering that Montreal upgrade, we got it on Ollie first."We decided to give the brake upgrade to Esteban first. Also, in terms of power steering, we had another upgrade on the power steering before shutdown in Budapest. We decided to give that to Esteban because, again, he was more vocal about it and he was struggling more [with] the power steering feel."The last two upgrades we gave it to Esteban, so this time around, it's back to Ollie."Komatsu said "we don't have any hidden agenda" because there's "no point bulls***ting" when telling the drivers about it. Early-race phase will be critical for CadillacCadillac's battle with its brakes continues after myriad overheating problems this year.Valtteri Bottas has previously characterised this as a mixture of airflow and component problems, and on Thursday referred to "even more robust material than before in the brake ducts" available here as a key area of improvement. Monza should not pose a brake-cooling challenge in normal running, but he highlighted the early laps of the Italian GP as the critical phase for this."In our numbers, we should be OK but what is quite hard to simulate is the traffic effect, especially if there's multiple cars in a train," said Botas. "That's when you get the lack of airflow on the straights. So I would say the first part of the race is going to be the most critical for us."There are still "further steps to make in terms of the pure airflow", but Cadillac has made significant progress in improving this weakness.However, it was only two races ago, in Hungary, that Bottas retired with cooked brakes early on the 14th lap, having spent the early stages of the race in the queue behind Alex Albon's Williams. Virtually everyone quizzed about it has acknowledged that the slipstream effect will be supercharged here - which will no doubt influence qualifying, but will also intensify the nature of the "yo-yo race" that's widely expected to play out here.The expectation is one of deployment strategies converging in terms of the optimal lap - but that the actual race situation can create some crazy offsets."I don't actually know how it will play out. It's going to be massive yo-yo racing, really," reckoned Alex Albon."The thing is, you don't want to be in a situation where you come out of sync with everyone else and then you are kind of exposed to falling down the grid pretty quickly."I think the race pace side of things, what you'll see in FP1, FP2, will be drivers using overtake buttons, anti-buttons, playing around with creating almost fake racing scenarios, just to get some rhythm and experience on how to do it.""We started to look at it now since quite a few days and trying to understand," said Charles Leclerc. "It's also very, very difficult to predict because the thing is that once you are in the car, it always looks nice from outside - but the difference is sometimes is that much that it's very difficult to then react to the car in front.""I think the race is going to be chaos, especially at the beginning," said Oscar Piastri.There have also been some outlandish figures cited in terms of the benefit of a slipstream on a single laptime - but no real fear of a 2019-like Q1 farce.

item.title: 'He's on a really high level' – Felix Gall fails to convert attack into time gain as he's forced to concede to superior Enric Mas again at Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: It's quite clear that Decathlon CMA CGM have the strongest mountain train at the ongoing Vuelta a España, with Matthew Riccitello, Callum Scotson, and Gregor Mühlberger all making it to the final climb on Thursday's brutal stage 12 to support Felix Gall.But once the Austrian made his move on the lower slopes up to Calar Alto, he was once again unable to distance the rider he is most trying to gain time on, GC leader Enric Mas (Movistar), who eventually counterattacked Gall and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) to extend his lead.Ever since Mas went into the red jersey after Tadej Pogačar crashed out on stage 8, he's answered every question asked of him, mostly coming from the Decathlon rider, who could only acknowledge the physical and mental strength shown by the Spaniard, who now sits 1:45 ahead of Roglič and 2:05 in front of Gall."He [Mas] went at the perfect moment, and he's on a really high level," said Gall at the finish. "He showed it from the beginning, super solid. I mean, he seems to be managing the red jersey well, and also mentally he's doing a really good job."Gall's demeanour wasn't obviously one of disappointment, though, and his words matched that, detailing how today's stage was more about solidifying his podium spot against the likes of Roglič and Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos), which he did, now with a 1:43 lead over Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) in fourth."The goal was to drop one of the guys who are currently in contention for the podium, and unfortunately Oscar crashed, but we could drop him, and that's basically all that we wanted to do today. From our side, it was a good day."I had to do a lot of work on the climb, but it was for sure a brutal day. It was so hot, and you could also see there were not many guys left in the end, but I'm managing it also. For sure, I feel fatigued now, but all so far so good."Gall's next chance to try and impose himself on his GC rivals will come over his favoured terrain on Saturday to Sierra de la Pandera, a 12km brute which averages 7.2% gradient. However, if today's performances were anything to go by, it will be Mas who is on top again, not Gall, who is looking likely to finish with a second Grand Tour podium in 2026 after his runner-up placing at the Giro d'Italia.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: What's behind Haas's uncomfortable engine upgrade split at Italian GP
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Haas faces an unusual situation at the Italian Grand Prix with only one of its drivers getting Ferrari's upgraded Formula 1 engine.With Ferrari introducing its 'ADUO 2' step for both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, available under F1's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities mechanism for engine manufacturers, its customer teams have been told that there is only one available for each of them right now.Cadillac has elected to not run it on either of its cars in Italy, but Haas felt the opportunity of more power at the high-speed Monza circuit was too good a chance to pass up.In going for the engine, Haas faced the unenviable task of having to pick which of its drivers would get it. In the end it was decided that it would go to Ollie Bearman.Team principal Ayao Komatsu explained that the decision to give Bearman the nod was due to Ocon having had priority with recent developments.Brake improvements and changes to the power steering made before the summer break were given to Ocon first, so Haas felt it was only fair to give Bearman the new power unit at Monza.Komatsu admitted that the situation was not ideal and was actually something it avoided previously when Ferrari's first ADUO step came in Austria at the end of June.Back then, Haas delayed introducing the engine upgrade until both cars could have it."Last time around we didn't do that, we waited until we had enough engines to introduce both drivers together," he said."But this time, obviously, Monza is a very power-sensitive circuit so it's a shame to have performance sitting in a garage, right? But, yeah, of course it makes it very challenging [having only one available]."It would have been better if two engines are available at least. But, again, Ferrari is pushing like hell to get as much performance on the engine as possible."Of course, they want to introduce it at Monza for the reasons I just said to you. So that means they've got the minimum quantity just to satisfy the regulation."Komatsu said that while it was not ideal for Haas having to pick a driver for the power unit, it was important that the reasoning behind it was explained clearly to both drivers."You just have to be transparent about it," he said. "We operate in as transparent and as fair a manner as possible."Now, of course, you can't please everyone every time, but we don't have any hidden agenda, we don't have any personal agenda for one driver or another."We've been building that relationship up, so of course, Esteban won't be happy not to get the PU number four straight away. But this is the best for the team and then this is the fairest way we can do it."Haas has only ended up with one upgraded Ferrari power unit because manufacturers do not have to supply customer teams with more than that when they introduce a new specification.F1's technical regulations state that if a new homologation step comes into play, then a manufacturer must make it "available to each F1 team supplied by the PU manufacturer at the competition at which it is first introduced with at least one power unit of the new homologation specification".The requirement for at least one new spec to be available will be to ensure that customer teams get some parity with works squads when modifications are made.If manufacturers were forced to supply two fresh engines to each partner team, then that would impose an extra burden on those that have a large number of customer outfits, which could delay the introduction of a new step in the first place.How much is the new engine worth?Ferrari has been eager to play down how big an impact its ADUO 2 engine will make on the pecking order.Team principal Fred Vasseur said ahead of the Italian GP weekend: "It represents a step in the right direction and as we know this year is very much about marginal gains."However, Ocon suggested that, based on what he has been told, he expected there to be a notable difference between the old and new power units."I'm going to be driving with the old engine, so that's going to be quite some loss," he said.Ferrari's upgraded engine is understood to feature a larger turbo that features other key modifications to its design aimed at improving power.It initially went for a smaller turbo at the start of this season because it felt a more responsive power unit would give it a big advantage at race starts.However, the deficit rivals faced with turbo lag was reduced a lot by revisions made to the start procedure - so Ferrari's advantage here was wiped away.A larger turbo should help boost overall power. And although the differences are unlikely to be a game-changer, Hamilton reckoned that it would help cover some of the deficit that has been faced this year."Every little helps," he said. "Up until this point of the year, even in the last race on such a short circuit, we were losing four tenths a lap through the race. So that's a huge deficit and we've carried that through the year to this point."This is a step forward. It's not the whole gap that we need, but we knew that would be the case. But to see bits coming each weekend, adding to the car, it's exciting to see that we are pushing and strongly still believe that we've got what it takes to win."

item.title: Clarke Schmidt is getting ready to give Yankees’ bullpen a boost
item.author: Andrés Chávez
item.content:encoded: The Yankees can use all the relief pitching help they can get these days. Due to injuries, it seems like they are always improvising to fill the unit with reliable arms, signing or claiming guys such as Justin Topa (already DFA’d), Michael Fulmer, and John Schreiber in the last week or so.They need some stability in the mid-to-late innings. Fortunately, one of their homegrown guys is getting ready and shaping up as an option at the right time: Clarke Schmidt. At the moment, Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Will Warren, and Elmer Rodríguez are ahead of the 2017 first-round pick in the rotation depth chart, with Ryan Weathers potentially rejoining the staff in a few weeks, too. That’s why the organization has already said Schmidt is ticketed for the bullpen when he returns.To be fair, that’s probably where he’s needed the most. The Yankees’ rotation is better than their bullpen, and they could certainly use an established starter with (successful) relief pitching experience to get through some of the toughest outs in the late innings.Schmidt, who moved his rehab to Triple-A and pitched two solid innings in which he allowed one run and struck out three on Wednesday, already had a strong season as a bullpen piece back in 2022. That year, he pitched 29 games, starting just three, and posted a 3.12 ERA and a 3.60 FIP in 57.2 innings. He walked 23 and struck out 56.While it’s true that Schmidt didn’t have a good postseason that year, allowing three runs (and two homers) in three games and 2.1 innings, he is much more mature at this point in his career. After that showing, he has logged three seasons as a starter with mixed but mostly positive results.A role in relief would allow Schmidt to throw harder in short spurts and maybe focus on some specific pitches, such as the cutter, the knuckle curve, the slider, and the sweeper, with a few four-seamers sprinkled in.After posting a 26.3 percent strikeout rate in 2024 and a 23.1 mark last year as a starter, Schmidt has some exciting strikeout potential as a reliever, throwing fewer innings at max effort, with the pitching know-how he has gotten over the years. God knows the Yankees need someone who can get some swings and misses in the back of the bullpen.It’s unclear if manager Aaron Boone will use him as a traditional one-inning reliever or as a multi-inning weapon, but he can thrive in any role. For that to happen, however, he needs to get through his rehab without any setbacks.Before the two solid frames he racked up on Wednesday for the RailRiders, he had only pitched one game in Double-A, surrendering two runs in 0.2 frames. He is still working his way back from a long layoff following elbow surgery last year, and it stands to reason that he could be rusty whenever he returns to the bigs.Since Schmidt won’t be starting this year, or at least that’s not the plan at the moment, he is not expected to need too many additional rehab appearances before being ready for activation. In fact, depending on how he feels, there’s a tiny chance his next outing comes in the majors, even though it’s unlikely.He’ll probably return to starting next year. For now, however, he will help a unit that has the best ERA in the league this season at 3.08, but was 11th with a 3.67 mark in August. As good as the relief corps has been as a whole, the group clearly could use support now, and Schmidt is solid bet to provide it.

item.title: Why Monza, F1's "Temple of Speed", could be slower than the Hungaroring
"Gentle with the throttle pedal" – Verstappen mentally prepared for painful Monza weekend
Why Norris has started his own racing team
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris has explained the logic for creating his own racing team and driver development scheme - the first of which had "over a few hundred job requests" within an hour of being announced.Ahead of the Italian GP, Norris launched LN4 Fusion - a single-seater racing team that will compete in Formula 4, Formula 3 and (pending approval) Formula 2 - as well as the separate LN4 Legacy Programme, a talent scheme led by ex-Alpine sporting director Julian Rouse.On Thursday at Monza, Norris explained how it had happened earlier in his career than he thought was possible."I wouldn't say we've [Norris and his personal team] ever spoken about it properly, but we've always kind of thought it would be a cool idea to do at some point," Norris explained."I probably didn't think it'd be something I'd do this early on. Certain things came together, and certain groups came together. Opportunities arose from that."It's been a lengthy process from when we started to speak about it, which was already last year, into turning it into a thing this year. So I don't know if that's a long time or not in terms of creating something like this."But I think the main thing is, we've just got a lot of pretty experienced people from kind of all directions. We've been able to piece things together pretty quickly, I would say. That's been a great thing."'Hundreds of applications'Norris's new racing team has already received strong interest, as it looks to rapidly build up teams to compete across F1's junior ladder."The reactions have been great. I know [LN4 Fusion team principal] Rene [Rosin] said he got over a few hundred job requests within an hour or so of the announcement," Norris added."There's a lot of attraction from a range of drivers, but also mechanics, engineers, all the people that make a team, a big team. I'm proud as an individual, but also proud that we've been able to put something very special together."Norris already has a strong recruit in team principal Rosin, who took the Prema team that his father co-founded to the majority of its 40-plus championship titles, before the family's sudden exit last year.Prior to that, Prema was the benchmark team on the ladder, and one which Norris spent a lot of his pre-F1 career racing against - breaking Prema's six-year F3 title streak with Carlin in 2017."A lot of the guys are people I've known for a long time. I've known Rene for many years, and I have raced against Prema since F4, so back in 2015," Norris recalled."I've known of him very well, and I know him personally reasonably well, and so do my team around me."So we wanted to put together a group that is experienced and knows how to lead a team - and not just create one good team, whether that's just in F3 or just in F2, but be able to put together a project and something long-term, know how to bring people together."I've also been able to experience over the course of the last seven years what makes a good leader, what makes a good team, and a lot of it starts with the person at the very top, and he is that person."Just a very nice guy, a guy you can just enjoy having a good chat with, but a guy who also loves doing what he does, which is winning and creating a successful team, bringing people together, maximising things."So he was the inevitable choice at the end of the day. He was available, and he was the guy we wanted."Norris's McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri, who won his F3 and F2 titles with Prema, said: "I've got great memories with Rene, the Rosin family at Prema as well."I can't really speak highly enough of that family as people and also the success they're able to have."I'm certainly not expecting that team to be slow, that's for sure."Another Prema F1 graduate, Ollie Bearman, called it a "cool initiative" and said: "He's picked a very good person to run the team in Rene."He led the most successful junior team in history. So really nice to see him back."I'm really happy about that, and I hope he can also continue that legacy for himself, for his father as well, for his family. It's something really, really cool."Williams driver Alex Albon expressed surprise at how Norris is able to fit in such a big project while racing."Yes, I would," Albon said when The Race asked him if he'd like to do something similar."It's impressive in many ways, because I feel like I've got way too much on my plate, just trying to do this sport, never mind other championships as well."But it's very cool to do. I think it's noble to see his work being put back into the roots of it all."Whether that's sooner rather than later, I don't know, but I'd love to do something - maybe not race teams, but working out a way to help kids either get better or get their chances in motorsports."For Norris, it's all about the strong team that he has around him - the same team that enabled him to pull off a successful 'Landostand' at the British Grand Prix and other off-track activities.They ensure Norris can still focus on his day job while maximising his branding - the striking dayglow yellow - and him being a big draw which can bring investors to the table."A lot of this stuff goes on in the background," Norris said. "I've also been able to really focus on just doing my own job and focus on driving fast."So I'm pleased that it can be something that can run very separately to me."We have great people running the whole thing, but I can also just be part of it when I'm able to. It's been great."Helping drivers one-by-oneAlongside the racing team is the LN4 Legacy Programme that is more focused on picking out young drivers and taking them all the way to F1."The Legacy Programme is more to pick out individuals, people that I believe can get to F1, and we believe can get to F1, and try and help them one at a time," Norris said."That's our initial goal, when you say hundreds of thousands, you're still talking about millions of dollars to help one person."When you say to help a much bigger group, you're talking about needing a lot more money. We've got to start somewhere, and I'm happy that I'm trying to help at least one to begin with, and then we'll work on two, and then three, and then four, and five."But the bigger project is not just what one thing can one driver do? If you want to help bigger areas and economies that are just worse to start racing and allow people to start their dream, it's much bigger than just me doing my job and trying to help out on that."That takes the sport itself, that takes a lot more work from F1, from FIA, from karting companies. It's just simply too expensive, so you cannot rely on people just to fund more people. You have to find other ways to make it more friendly for people to start racing, especially financially."You've got to lower the costs somehow of teams, of the ability to go testing, of just signing up to do F2. F2 is over $2million, or €2m I think, to start. You've got to start somewhere."My ability is starting with one, and that's already a big project, and I think bigger than what people expect, but I want to expand on that. That takes time."Obviously, I have my own go-kart. I know other drivers, and Daniel [Ricciardo] and so forth have started projects to get more kids into racing. That's certainly my plan, but this is the beginning of it."With time and with more partners coming on board, and more money, more support, we can turn it into a way of helping more people from around the world."Norris isn't the only one...Plenty of drivers like Albon expressed an interest in doing something similar, but one driver is forming their own driver development project: Cadillac's Sergio Perez."It's really nice what Lando has done. From my side, I'm also at the point of my career that I would like to do something," Perez said."I'm preparing something with my manager, Khalil [Beschir], for the near term."We will be able to share that in the next few months - but we are definitely working on something from our side because we would like to give back to the sport and help the younger generations as well."

item.title: Oscar Onley suffers huge dent to Vuelta a España podium hopes after early crash and summit finish struggles
item.content:encoded: Oscar Onley (Netcompany-Ineos) suffered a big blow to his podium hopes at the Vuelta a España, crashing early on stage 12 before struggling on the summit finish at Calar Alto. The British rider started the day fourth overall, 41 seconds off the podium, but has now slipped to fifth place at 4:29 behind leader Enric Mas (Movistar).Onley was dropped when Felix Gall kicked off the hostilities on the hardest part of the Calar Alto climb, which measured 17.5km at 5.6%, but with early steep slopes ahead of some more gentle sections near the top.Onley had been part of a GC group that was reduced to eight by Gall's Decathlon CMA CGM teammates, but couldn't follow when the race really ignited.Initially, he chased with Richard Carapaz, but the EF Education-EasyPost rider managed to work his way back across to a group containing Gall and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), second and third on GC, who were chasing a long-range attack from the race leader Enric Mas (Movistar).Onley, however, only lost more ground as the climb went on. He crossed the lined 2:09 down on Mas, and 1:42 down on the trio of Gall, Roglič, and Carapaz.He's now 2:23 adrift of the podium, where Gall sits in third, and didn't have too much of an explanation for his losses. "I think physically, in my legs and stuff, I felt OK, I just couldn't really go that deep today. I just had to kind of ride my own pace," he told after the stage, before praising work from his teammate"When I caught up with Jack [Haig] he did a really good job to save some time and help me really recover on that flat section, so he did really good."Onley remains in the white jersey as the best young rider, but he now has a lead of only 30 seconds, with Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) making strides after his stage victory from the breakaway.It remains to be seen how badly Onley was affected by his early crash, but he was left heavily dusted up by the incident, which occurred with some 130km left to race.Onley was on the side of the peloton that was taking the left-hand side around a large roundabout, and he slid out, sliding along the tarmac on his right-hand side and onto the grass at the side of the road.The crash was fairly random, and Onley himself didn't really know what happened."I have no idea. One minute you're on the bike and the next you're sliding along the ground. I guess the roads here are pretty slippy."He was visibly frustrated as he got back to his feet and got a spare bike, before teammates helped him close the gap to the peloton. He then visited the medical car to get some of his road rash looked at. For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Vuelta a España Stage 12: Enric Mas Goes Long as ‘Mini-Pogačar’ Omrzel Wins Big
item.author: ahood
item.content:encoded: Enric Mas attacked with 11km to go in a brutal climbing stage to distance his GC rivals while Slovenian talent Omrzel wins 'queen stage.'

item.title: Vuelta a España: Jakob Omrzel wins stage 12 as Enric Mas has another stellar ride on Calar Alto
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: As the Vuelta a España headed back into the mountains and the summit finish at Calar Alto, it was Enric Mas (Movistar) who once again proved the strongest of the GC riders, adding more time to his overall lead with an attack 12km from the finish.Red jersey hopefuls Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) had no answer to Mas' move, with Mas cannily linking up with Movistar teammate from the break, Raúl García Pierna.Gall and Roglič, too, got help from teammates dropping back – Léo Bisiaux and Luke Tuckwell – and a resurgent Gregor Mühlberger. The strength in numbers behind the solo Mas seemingly had no effect, though, with the chasers only losing time as the finish neared.Mas eventually crossed the line with another 27 seconds in the bag, extending his lead over Roglič to 1:45, while Gall now lies at 2:06 down.The GC battle wasn't the fight for stage victory, however. That played out minutes up the road as 20-year-old Vuelta debutant Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) broke clear of what was once a 30-man breakaway group with 11.7km to go. Holding a four-minute lead over Mas and co, he left behind Urko Berrade (Kern Pharma) to go solo to the finish.Omrzel's power was such that even the big GC moves behind barely made a dent in his lead. He hit the final kilometre with a three-minute lead over Mas, and the 2025 Giro Next Gen winner duly converted it to the biggest win of his young career.2024 Vuelta stage winner Berrade crossed the line in second place, 1:56 down, while mountain classification leader Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) took third, 2:13 back. Mas wouldn't add bonus seconds to his total at the line, finishing in sixth, 2:56 down.Omrzel's ride, which saw him in virtual second overall at one point, saw him leap from 10th to sixth overall, 4:59 behind Mas. While the podium trio stayed in place, Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) moved up to third as he finished alongside Gall and Roglič. The Ecuadorian leapfrogged Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos), who dropped away further down the climb to finish 5:05 adrift of Omrzel and 2:09 behind Mas."I'm not surprised because I know how much work I put in, and I knew that these days were going to come sooner or later. But for sure, I was not expecting 100% to do it on my first Grand Tour," Omrzel, who now lies 30 seconds off Onley's white jersey, said after his win."So, I mean, I still can't believe what I did, but I felt super good. I'm still feeling okay. I'm not tired, so I don't know, I'm just enjoying it at the moment."The team behind us is really great. As riders, we understand each other really well, and at the moment, we are working so well together. The whole team is just perfection."We said that we are playing PlayStation, and that's what we are doing at the moment! Whatever we want, we do. We go in the breakaway with Pello [Bilbao], Santi Buitrago], and the other guys. It's just amazing, and I'm really proud of that."After Wednesday's sprint finish in Lorca, the Vuelta a España peloton headed back to the mountains for the 166.6km stage 12 with five classified climbs and 4,500 metres of elevation on the road to Calar Alto (17km at 5.6%).Early third-category ascents including the Alto de Cabecico (8km at 3.3%) and the Alto de Cóbdar (5km at 4.5%) led on to the mid-stage second-category climb, the Collado Garcia (19km at 2.4%). The first-category Alto de Velefique (13km at 7.2%) lay 29km from the line ahead of the stage's final ascent.Georg Steinhauser (EF Education-EasyPost) put in the first major attack of the day, though a solo breakaway on such a tough stage was never likely to stick. More attacks followed after the German was caught, including efforts from João Almeida (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and points leader Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike).That move, too, was brought back, before Van Aert jumped clear once more on the Alto de Cabecico to grab three mountain points, moving one point nearer to KOM leader Buitrago.It would take some 40km for the breakaway to properly go, as 30 riders jumped clear before the Alto de Cóbdar. Almeida, Van Aert, and Buitrago were up there again. The trio were joined by a host of other notable names, including Mas' teammates Raúl García Pierna and Pablo Castrillo, Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Luke Tuckwell (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Léo Bisiaux (Decathlon CMA CGM), Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello-Q36.5), Urko Berrade (Kern Pharma), Jack Haig (Netcompany Ineos), Marco Brenner (Tudor), Mauri Vansevenant (Soudal-QuickStep), Alexey Lutsenko (NSN), plus Andreas Leknessund, and Tobias Halland Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility).Omrzel was also in the move, the 20-year-old a GC danger man lying 10th overall at 8:05 down. Movistar and Red Bull lined up at the head of the peloton behind, leaving the break to race over two minutes clear.At the Alto de Cóbdar, the gap was up over four minutes as Van Aert led the race over the top to collect six points to Buitrago's four, moving closer in the mountain classification standings once again.From there, the road kept on gradually rising, stop-start, to the Collado Garcia. Again it was Van Aert vs Buitrago at the top, and again, Van Aert led the way. The Belgian took five points to the Colombian's three, putting him at 30 to 38 in the KOM standings.With 80km and two climbs left to tackle, the break enjoyed a six-minute lead, a gap that reached 7:30 in the valley road – putting Omrzel up to virtual second place overall.Up ahead, Almeida gave his all on the uphill towards the Alto de Velefique as Van Aert grabbed 20 points at the intermediate sprint. The Portuguese rider's effort helped split apart the breakaway group, while further back, race leader Enric Mas was down to a single helper in Iván Romeo, with Castrillo and García Pierna still well up the road.On the climb itself, Carapaz was the first man to make a big attack. The Ecuadorian attacked with 37km to go, 6km from the top, quickly taking a 30-second lead over a GC group which counted only around 15 riders.Up front, 5:30 clear of Mas, Omrzel made a move to go clear. He took Bisiaux with him, the pair taking 20 seconds on the rest of the break. They were brought back a kilometre from the top, however, while further down, Romeo dragged back Carapaz, too.Buitrago led Lutsenko across the summit for another 10 mountain points to go clear of Van Aert once more. They were joined by seven more at the front in Omrzel, Bisiaux, Berrade, Haig, Tuckwell, García Pierna, and Vansevenant.5:30 back, Castrillo had waited for the GC group to help Mas, while García Pierna slowed from the breakaway at the bottom of the climb to provide assistance later on. Romeo and Castrillo led the GC group onto the climb.Buitrago's early acceleration at the front blew the break apart for good, leaving just him, Omrzel, Bisiaux, and Berrade out front. In the GC group, Decathlon took over the pacemaking 15km from the top, quickly dropping Mattias Skjelmose (Lidl-Trek) and Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike).Gall launched soon afterwards, taking Mas and Roglič with him as Onley – who suffered a minor crash early in the stage – was dropped along with Carapaz.Buitrago and Bisiaux were dropped from the break before the end of the steep early section of the climb, leaving Omrzel and Berrade to lead the race into the final 12.5km. Omrzel was soon on his own, leaving Berrade behind with 11.7km to go.Four minutes down the mountain, it was Mas who decided to go solo, the red jersey once again attacking his GC rivals after winning stage 9 at the Alto de Aitana. The Spaniard leapt away to a half-minute lead before linking up with García Pierna 9km from the top.The pair held the chase behind at 40 seconds before García Pierna's work was done, 5km from the top. Further back, Tuckwell and Bisiaux had dropped back to help Gall and Roglič, while Carapaz and another Decathlon man, Mühlberger, caught back on.Despite having more numbers than the solo Mas, the chase group made few inroads into the Spaniard's lead. That initial 30-second gap remained, regardless of what was going on behind, and he danced towards the line in no danger of being brought back.Gall and Roglič found themselves alone again on the run towards the finish, having dropped Carapaz, but he made his way back to the duo before the finish, and the three men crossed the line having shed another 27 seconds to the GC leader.Omrzel had already long finished his ride, celebrating a major breakthrough victory two weeks into the first Grand Tour of his career.

item.title: Disastrously-timed puncture sees Filippo Ganna caught out in GC-ending split at Tour of Britain
item.content:encoded: Filippo Ganna saw his general classification hopes at the Tour of Britain go up in smoke on stage 2, as the Italian suffered a mechanical problem just as the peloton was splitting in the crosswinds. Despite the early crosswinds passing by without incident, the race suddenly came to life with 60km to go on Thursday's flat stage to Skegness, and the peloton split in two. Just as the two groups were splitting, Ganna, second overall after his runner-up finish on stage 1, appeared off the back of the race with his arm in the air, appealing for assistance for what looked to be a puncture.Former racer Geraint Thomas, who retired at last year's Tour of Britain and is now Netcompany-Ineos' Director of Racing, scrambled from the passenger seat of the team car to help. As a mechanic grabbed a new bike from the roof rack, Thomas delivered the push-off to get Ganna back up to speed. The damage, however, was done, and Ganna was left scrambling in group of around 50 riders, which quickly found itself almost a minute down on the main pack of 40, where the key sprinters and GC riders were all located. With the exception of their sprinter, Sam Welsford, Netcompany-Ineos put their whole squad in the second group to chase, with some assistance on hand from the Flanders-Baloise team. However, despite moving to within 30 seconds of the lead group with 35km to go, by which point they were in sight, the gap never closed. In fact, from there it only yawned out again amid the merciless pace-setting in the lead group, where the sprint teams, along with UAE Team Emirates-XRG – who don't have a sprinter but several GC cards – all rode hard and in unison. By 10km to go, the gap was back out to one minute and the cause was lost. Ganna eventually crossed the line in 67th place, 1:43 down on the front of the race. He drops to 10th overall, 1:53 down on the leader Lewis Askey (NSN Cycling)In a race that's expected to be decided by tight margins, with stage 4 the toughest day of the race but still light on climbing, Ganna had been considered among the possible contenders. And he'd made a strong start, powering up Michaelgate in Lincoln to place second on a stage that saw small gaps. Stage 1 winner) Askey remains in the overall lead, with UAE possessing a strong hand with Tim Wellens in second at 12 seconds.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
